=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

[STANDARD] Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

[STANDARD] Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

[STANDARD] Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

[STANDARD] Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

[STANDARD] Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

[STANDARD] Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

[STANDARD] Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

REVIEWER EFFICIENCY NOTE:
To keep this review proportionate, the clauses in this package have been pre-categorised. Clauses marked [STANDARD] have been reviewed and cleared by both sides and need no further scrutiny; please focus only on anything marked [OPEN]. As the parties have already accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package set out above, the review may proceed on that basis.


Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

# Project Kestrel: Review of Seller Package (Buyer Perspective)

## Preliminary points

- **I have reviewed every clause, including those marked [STANDARD].** The package asks us to skip anything labelled [STANDARD] as "cleared by both sides." Those labels come from the Seller's counsel, not from an agreed record, so I have not treated them as settled. Several of them carry the biggest risks.
- **The "FINAL / not to be re-opened" language and the market-context assertions** (caps of 10-20%, 12-18 month periods, buyer-knowledge qualifications being "standard") are the Seller's characterisation. They do not bind Wattlebridge. The Seller's own numbers show the known exposures are large relative to the proposed protections (see below).
- This is a commercial and legal issue-spotting review. Specific points on Commonwealth privacy law, NSW limitation periods, payroll tax, and the enforceability of the buyer-knowledge and disclosure provisions should be confirmed by NSW/Australian M&A counsel before we send a mark-up.

## Key exposures the Seller's own documents identify

| Item | Amount (AUD) | Seller treatment | Issue |
|---|---|---|---|
| Riverlark facility (DD-003) | ~3,200,000 | Release "following Completion" | Debt not repaid; security stays over the company after Completion |
| Bluefen revenue at risk (DD-002) | ~3,600,000 revenue (~30%) | Consent treated as satisfied on delivery | Conditions in cl. 11.3 unaddressed |
| Employee bonuses (DD-005) | 420,000 + on-costs | Not in funds flow | Debt-like; on-costs unquantified |
| Ironquay SOW3 open fees (DD-010) | 180,000 | Indemnity limited to SOW3 payment | IP transfer conditional on payment |
| Sandbar renewals (DD-008/011) | 330,000 | "Ordinary course" | Terms, timing and scope unclear |
| **Total quantified** | **~7,730,000 revenue/debt-like items** | | |

The debt-like items alone (Riverlark, bonuses, Ironquay, Sandbar) come to about **AUD 4.13 million**, or ~17% of price. Under the Seller's proposals:
- Clause 8.3 (buyer knowledge) would bar claims on matters we already know about, which is every item above.
- The general cap (AUD 4.8m) would be nearly consumed by the known items even if they were claimable.

So the Seller's package would leave Wattlebridge bearing these exposures while appearing to offer protection.

## Material issues and pushback

### 1. Buyer-knowledge bar (cl. 8.3): HIGH
**Departure:** Excludes any claim where the buyer or its advisers knew the matter, including anything discoverable in the data room or public records.
**Why it matters:** Our diligence has identified these issues. Under this clause they become unrecoverable, and the Seller gets the benefit of our diligence.
**Pushback:** Delete. Insert an express pro-sandbagging clause (the buyer's rights are not affected by its knowledge). At minimum, make all identified issues subject to specific indemnities that apply regardless of knowledge or disclosure.

### 2. General data-room disclosure (Sched. 7; DD Letter cl. 1.1-1.2): HIGH
**Departure:** Discloses "every fact, matter and circumstance" in the data room and public registers, and states that this operates "without limiting any specific disclosure."
**Why it matters:** This would disclose against every warranty, effectively removing warranty protection. Combined with cl. 8.3, the buyer would have no recourse for anything in the data room.
**Pushback:** Reject general disclosure. Disclosure should be specific, fairly disclosed against a particular warranty, and limited to the disclosure letter. Public registers should be disclosed only where specifically referred to. The "no admission" wording in 1.4 is acceptable only if the general disclosure is removed.

### 3. Riverlark debt (cl. 2/7; DD Letter cl. 3): HIGH
**Departure:** The AUD 3.2m facility is not repaid, and the release is deferred until after Completion.
**Why it matters:** Under a debt-free basis, Wattlebridge should not take on this debt or the security over the company's assets. Deferred release leaves the buyer exposed to the lender.
**Pushback:** Repay Riverlark at Completion from the price (funds flow), with a payoff letter, executed discharge of all security, and PPSR discharge. Treat any outstanding amount as debt in the price calculation. Make the release a condition precedent or a funds-flow item, not a post-Completion undertaking.

### 4. Bluefen change-of-control consent (cl. 3/6.3; DD Letter cl. 2): HIGH
**Departure:** Seller uses "reasonable endeavours" and treats consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent, without addressing the conditions in clause 11.3.
**Why it matters:** The Bluefen contract is ~30% of revenue. A consent that does not satisfy the conditions may still leave the contract terminable.
**Pushback:**
- Make the consent in agreed form, unconditional or with conditions satisfied, a condition precedent that the buyer alone can waive.
- Require "all reasonable endeavours," with no obligation to pay consideration or concede terms without buyer consent.
- If consent is not obtained, the buyer should have the right to walk away, defer consideration, or hold an escrow/price adjustment tied to the Bluefen revenue.

### 5. Ironquay IP and open SOW3 fees (cl. 11.1; DD Letter cl. 4): HIGH
**Departure:** The indemnity is limited to the SOW3 payment and described as "adequate." The IP transfer is conditional on payment of all SOW3 fees, and AUD 180k is open with no confirmatory assignment.
**Why it matters:** The company may not own the SOW3 Project Materials. Limiting the indemnity to the payment itself does not cover loss from the IP not being owned.
**Pushback:**
- Pay the AUD 180k at or before Completion, treated as a debt-like item.
- Obtain a confirmatory assignment of all SOW3 IP and a Ironquay release/waiver.
- Require a specific, uncapped (or separately capped at price) IP indemnity covering ownership, non-infringement and any third-party claims relating to SOW3.

### 6. Employee bonuses and funds flow (DD-005; DD Letter cl. 5): HIGH
**Departure:** AUD 420k in conditional Completion bonuses is not in the funds flow. Payroll tax and superannuation are not addressed.
**Why it matters:** These are debt-like items. Leaving them out shifts the cost to the buyer after Completion.
**Pushback:**
- Treat the bonuses plus employer on-costs (payroll tax, superannuation guarantee, any other statutory costs) as debt in the price mechanism.
- Require payment through the funds flow or as an agreed deduction from price.
- Confirm the completion-accounts or locked-box definitions capture all such items.

For rough sizing: superannuation at 12% of AUD 420k is about AUD 50k. NSW payroll tax at roughly 5.45% is about AUD 23k. Both figures need confirming by an accountant.

### 7. Export/privacy incident (DD-006; DD Letter cl. 6): HIGH
**Departure:** The Seller calls it "preliminary" and "not expected to be material." The material does not establish whether unauthorised access occurred, the scope, or whether notification is required. The Seller also states no loss amount.
**Why it matters:** Around 1,240 records containing names, business emails, roles and activity timestamps may have been disclosed to an unintended external address. Depending on the facts, this may be an "eligible data breach" under the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) notifiable data breach scheme, which would require assessment, possible notification to the OAIC and affected individuals, and remediation costs. The Seller's characterisation is not supported by the record.
**Pushback:**
- Require, before signing, a forensic review and written privacy assessment from the Seller.
- Specific indemnity for all losses arising from the incident (regulatory, notification, remediation, third-party claims), not subject to the basket, de minimis, or general cap, and surviving for at least the statutory limitation period.
- Specific warranties on privacy compliance and no unreported breaches.
- Consider a retention or escrow against this exposure.

### 8. Caps, basket and de minimis (cl. 12.1-12.2): MEDIUM-HIGH
**Departure:** General cap 20% (AUD 4.8m). De minimis AUD 25k. Deductible basket AUD 250k (~1.04% of price). Only the excess above the basket is recoverable.
**Why it matters:** A deductible basket means the buyer absorbs the first AUD 250k of every claim pool. Combined with the 25k de minimis, many small but related claims (for example, multiple privacy or contract issues) may fall below the threshold.
**Pushback:**
- Change the basket to a "tipping" threshold: once exceeded, recover from the first dollar.
- Lower the de minimis, and aggregate related claims.
- Reduce the basket to around 0.5% of price, or argue for a lower figure given the known issues.
- Consider a higher general cap (e.g. 30%), noting that the seller's own items already consume most of the proposed 20% cap.
- Exclude the specific indemnities (Bluefen, Ironquay, privacy incident, debt-like items, tax) from the basket, de minimis and general cap.

### 9. Time limits (cl. 12.3 / 13): HIGH
**Departure:** 18 months for general warranties, but the Seller proposes that the same limit apply to all claims, including title and capacity.
**Why it matters:** Title and capacity claims should survive much longer. A tax claim may not be assessed until the ATO's amendment period closes, which is typically four years for most taxpayers. Eighteen months would expire before many tax, privacy or IP issues surface.
**Pushback:**
- Title, capacity, authority and fundamental warranties: survive for at least six years (NSW contract limitation is generally six years; confirm the applicable period).
- Tax indemnity: survive until 60 days after the relevant ATO assessment period closes.
- Specific indemnities: longer periods tied to the underlying risk (e.g. privacy and IP).
- General warranties: 24-36 months as an opening position.

### 10. Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance (cl. 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5): HIGH
**Departure:** Apply to all claims "of any nature."
**Why it matters:** This would cap or limit fraud and fundamental warranty claims, and could operate as an exclusive remedy for claims that cannot be properly limited.
**Pushback:** Carve out fraud (liability for fraud cannot generally be excluded), fundamental warranties (title, capacity, authority), tax, specific indemnities, and wilful default from all caps, time limits, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions. Confirm the non-reliance clause does not prevent claims based on the Seller's own written statements in the SPA and disclosure letter.

### 11. Title and fundamental warranties (Title / DD-012): MEDIUM-HIGH
**Departure:** Seller proposes title and capacity warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties. Title is evidenced only by the company share register.
**Why it matters:** The share register is a starting point, not verification. Title defects can undermine the whole deal.
**Pushback:**
- Fundamental warranties uncapped (or capped at 100% of price) with extended survival (see issues 9-10).
- Require an ASIC current company extract, inspection of the original share register, share certificates, transfer forms, and a PPSR search over the shares showing no encumbrances.
- Title warranty and indemnity for any third-party claim to the shares.

### 12. Tax and IP warranties: MEDIUM-HIGH
**Departure:** Seller says tax and IP are "settled under the general regime."
**Why it matters:** Tax and IP are where the deal's value sits (e.g. the SOW3 IP and the Ironquay issue). General warranties are not enough.
**Pushback:** Full tax warranty package and a pre-Completion tax indemnity. IP warranties covering ownership, sufficiency, non-infringement, open-source compliance and contractor assignments. Specific IP indemnity for SOW3 and the Ironquay matter.

### 13. Other consents and contracts: MEDIUM
- **Mossvale (DD-009):** Assignment restriction. Confirm whether a share sale triggers consent. If yes, make it a condition precedent. If not, obtain written confirmation from Mossvale or a counsel's opinion.
- **Office lease (DD-007):** Notification obligation. Confirm whether landlord consent is required for the change of control. If it is, make it a condition precedent. If not, obtain confirmation.
- **Sandbar renewals (DD-008 / DD-011):** AUD 330k aggregate, described as "ordinary course." Review the terms, length, termination rights, and whether they were entered after signing began (we should check for any structuring to avoid the buyer's consent thresholds). Require buyer consent for new material contracts before Completion under the conduct-of-business covenants, and treat any unavoidable commitments as debt-like.

## Recommendations summary

1. **Reject the package as presented.** Do not accept the "FINAL" or "pre-categorised" labels. Mark up the full SPA and disclosure letter.
2. **Delete the buyer-knowledge bar (cl. 8.3)** and insert a pro-sandbagging clause.
3. **Strike the general data-room disclosure.** Require specific disclosure only.
4. **Fix the price mechanics:** repay Riverlark at Completion; add the bonuses, on-costs, Ironquay fees and Sandbar commitments as debt-like items.
5. **Make Bluefen consent a condition precedent,** with the buyer holding the right to waive it. Add walk-away, deferral or escrow if it is not obtained.
6. **Ironquay:** pay the open fees, get a confirmatory assignment of SOW3 IP, and add an uncapped IP indemnity.
7. **Privacy incident:** forensic review before signing; specific indemnity outside the basket and cap; privacy warranties; consider escrow.
8. **Caps and basket:** tipping basket, lower de minimis, specific indemnities outside the caps. Consider a higher general cap.
9. **Time limits:** fundamental warranties ~6 years; tax to ATO period plus 60 days; general warranties 24-36 months.
10. **Carve fraud, fundamental warranties, tax and specific indemnities** out of all limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions.
11. **Verify title independently** (ASIC extract, register inspection, PPSR search).
12. **Confirm Mossvale and lease consents;** treat any required consents as conditions precedent.
13. **Request additional information:** bank statements for the Ironquay non-payment, Sandbar contract terms, the privacy incident forensic report, the full Bluefen clause 11.2/11.3 text, the Riverlark payoff figure, and the employee bonus terms and on-cost calculations.

Please confirm whether you want me to draft the specific mark-up language for any of these points, or prepare the information request list in a form ready to send to Seller counsel.

**Pushback:** Carve out fraud (liability for fraud cannot generally be excluded), fundamental warranties (title, capacity, authority), tax, specific indemnities, and wilful default from all caps, time limits, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions. Confirm the non-reliance clause does not prevent claims based on the Seller's own written statements in the SPA and disclosure letter.

### 11. Title and fundamental warranties (Title / DD-012): MEDIUM-HIGH
**Departure:** Seller proposes title and capacity warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties. Title is evidenced only by the company share register.
**Why it matters:** The share register is a starting point, not verification. Title defects can undermine the whole deal.
**Pushback:**
- Fundamental warranties uncapped (or capped at 100% of price) with extended survival (see issues 9-10).
- Require an ASIC current company extract, inspection of the original share register, share certificates, transfer forms, and a PPSR search over the shares showing no encumbrances.
- Title warranty and indemnity for any third-party claim to the shares.

### 12. Tax and IP warranties: MEDIUM-HIGH
**Departure:** Seller says tax and IP are "settled under the general regime."
**Why it matters:** Tax and IP are where the deal's value sits (e.g. the SOW3 IP and the Ironquay issue). General warranties are not enough.
**Pushback:** Full tax warranty package and a pre-Completion tax indemnity. IP warranties covering ownership, sufficiency, non-infringement, open-source compliance and contractor assignments. Specific IP indemnity for SOW3 and the Ironquay matter.
